Perhaps the two best teams in Sac-Joaquin Section Division V, Sutter Union and Bear River High, won’t meet again until the SJS postseason next month. It’s likely to be a primetime clash of championship contenders just as last year’s was when Sutter and Bear River met in the D-V final in 2025 at Cosumnes River College. Sutter sits 23-5 and tops in MaxPreps’ D-5 poll, updated weekly through November. The Huskies are loaded across the court beginning with a superior trifecta at the pin positions: Alyvia Brown, Kenzy Shannon, Sissy Luttrell and Taylor Palmer are each having dominant 2026 seasons through about the halfway point of round one in the Golden Empire League. Luttrell leads Sutter, and is No. 6 in the division, with a .327 attack percentage. Brown hovers around .300, at .292, heading into next week, which opens Monday night at Casa Roble. Shannon sits just outside the top-10 in attack percentage, yet is top-5 in kills (151) and digs (149). Brown ended Sutter’s unbeaten week in the GEL three kills (148) away from Shannon. Palmer, Sutter’s No. 1 middle option, is No. 4 in the division with 155 kills. All the weapons are assisted by Kalena DeLaCerna, who sits top-3 in D-V with 343 setter assists. Bear River, No. 2 in the division behind Sutter, has weapons draped all across the top-5 in each offensive and defensive category. The Bruins will be in Yuba County on Monday to tackle Marysville, which sits top-15 in D-IV. River Valley, which suffered back-to-back tight losses to fall into the eight position in the MaxPreps D-III poll, is led in part by senior Parveen Takhar, who is closing in on 200 kills this fall. Her counterpart from across the net, Madison Jackson (Yuba City) sits at 182 kills heading into next week opening at D-IV No. 4 Placer Tuesday night.  Bridget Lavy (Yuba City) rounds out the division’s top-10 with 139 kills. YC ended the week at No. 3 in the poll. A new rankings version will be unveiled Sunday night into Monday by MaxPreps.com. River Valley freshman Molly Squires is No. 2 in the division with 349 assists. She leads her counterpart from across town, Athziri Romero (Yuba City) by 50 assists heading into the weekend. Alexandra Garcia of Wheatland Union, stands top-10 with 222 assists. The Pirates are fighting for a top-3 spot out in the Pioneer Valley League, which has been won by Bear River three years in a row. title: Roberto Mancini says boos ‘normal’ after Italy’s disappointing loss v Belgium - Yahoo Sports
content: Italy picked up a disappointing 2-0 defeat against Belgium at the Stadio Olimpico in their opening UEFA Nations League game. The loss was met with boos as the performance was largely disappointing. Belgium largely dominated the first half and while Italy attempted to come into the game in the second half, it was clear who the better team was. Chaos did break out at the end of the tie but this was drowned out by the boos. Manager Roberto Mancini spoke to Rai about the game and made it clear that the boos are understandable considering the performance. The manager said – via TMW: "Belgium played better than us in the first half, but they struggled in the second. We could have equalized, but then we conceded due to our own mistakes." When asked specifically about the boos, Mancini said: "When we lose, we're not happy; boos are normal." He also emphasised that Italy were indeed poor in the first half, saying: "The first half was good, but the second was bad: the team played very well until the counterattack that made it 2-0. Belgium is a great team and played well." The Azzurri take on Turkey in the next game which could be a way to show that they're a better team than what they showed today. After that, they will take on France in what will be a more challenging game.

title: Overcoming IRS Statute of Limitations Defenses: An Analysis of Informal Claims and Disaster Relief in Singh v. United States - Current Federal Tax Developments
content: A site devoted to articles on current developments in federal taxes geared toward CPAs in tax practice. Juliet R. Singh v. United States, No. 1:25-cv-00056 (E.D.N.Y. Sept. 24, 2026) Tax practitioners frequently encounter situationally complex client cases where taxpayers, acting without immediate legal or tax counsel, submit informal written requests to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) explaining economic hardships or casualty events. When formal amended returns (Form 1040-X) are subsequently submitted past the standard statutory period under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 6511(a), the IRS routinely asserts a lack of subject matter jurisdiction under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(1), claiming sovereign immunity. In Juliet R. Singh v. United States, No. 1:25-cv-00056 (E.D.N.Y. Sept. 24, 2026), United States District Judge Ann M. Donnelly issued a pivotal ruling denying the government’s motion to dismiss for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. The decision provides critical guidance for Certified Public Accountants (CPAs) and Enrolled Agents (EAs) on two distinct legal theories preserving refund jurisdiction: the Informal Claim Doctrine and statutory postponements under IRC § 7508A(d) resulting from federally declared disasters. In October 2017, the taxpayer, Juliet R. Singh, fell victim to an online dating scam. The perpetrator fraudulently induced her to withdraw $100,000 from her Individual Retirement Account (IRA) and wire the funds to him under the guise of paying for emergency medical care. Following the transfer, the scammer ceased communications. Ms. Singh reported the crime to the New York City Police Department (NYPD) and the United States Secret Service, but law enforcement was unable to recover the funds or apprehend the perpetrator. On April 11, 2018, Ms. Singh filed a timely federal individual income tax return (Form 1040) for the 2017 tax year. Although IRC § 165 permits tax deductions for uncompensated theft losses, Ms. Singh—unaware of the proper tax accounting treatment—did not claim a theft loss deduction on her return. Instead, she reported the entire $100,000 IRA withdrawal as taxable gross income and paid a total tax liability of $28,069.74 on June 14, 2018, which included a 10% early distribution penalty under IRC § 72(t). On July 15, 2019, the IRS Automated Underreporter (AUR) system in Holtsville, New York, issued a Notice CP2000 proposing an additional tax assessment of $4,547 plus interest, alleging an unreported $10,700 portion of her IRA distribution. In response: From 2020 through early 2023, Ms. Singh repeatedly telephoned and mailed follow-up letters to the IRS. On September 19, 2022, the IRS sent a letter acknowledging a “claim received on July 25, 2019,” but erroneously referenced the audit figure of $10,700 and stated: “The law allows you to file a claim for a refund of taxes you have paid. However, the law doesn’t allow you to file a claim to reduce the tax you owe.” The IRS instructed her to file an amended return. On October 7, 2022 (received by the IRS on October 19, 2022), Ms. Singh submitted a Form 1040-X for tax year 2017, requesting a $30,601 refund. On the form, she removed the $100,000 distribution from income and noted “1099-R should not be taxed,” attaching detailed cover letters and police report references explaining the theft loss. On August 15, 2023, the IRS disclaimed jurisdiction and denied her claim as untimely under IRC § 6511(a), asserting that her deadline expired on May 17, 2021. Following administrative appeal attempts, Ms. Singh filed a civil suit in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of New York on March 27, 2025. Ms. Singh’s complaint sought a full refund of $30,601 in federal income taxes and early withdrawal penalties paid for the 2017 tax year, along with statutory interest pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 2411 and IRC § 6611. The government moved to dismiss under FRCP 12(b)(1), asserting that sovereign immunity barred the action because no formal administrative refund claim was filed within the three-year period established by IRC § 6511(a). In federal tax litigation, the United States possesses sovereign immunity unless explicitly waived by statute (Block v. North Dakota ex rel. Board of Univ. & School Lands, 461 U.S. 273 (1983); Humphrey v. IRS, 2022 WL 17728194 (2d Cir. 2022)). Congress granted federal district courts original jurisdiction over tax refund actions under 28 U.S.C. § 1346(a)(1). However, this waiver is conditioned upon strict compliance with administrative prerequisites set forth in IRC § 7422(a): “No suit or proceeding shall be maintained in any court for the recovery of any internal revenue tax... until a claim for refund or credit has been duly filed with the Secretary, according to the provisions of law in that regard, and the regulations of the Secretary established in pursuance thereof.” Treasury Regulation § 301.6402-2(b)(1) requires that a claim set forth in detail each ground upon which a credit or refund is claimed, along with supporting facts under penalties of perjury. Under IRC § 6511(a), a claim must be filed within three years from the date the return was filed or two years from the time the tax was paid, whichever is later (AmBase Corp. v. United States, 731 F.3d 109 (2d Cir. 2013)). To defeat the government’s FRCP 12(b)(1) motion, the taxpayer asserted three independent legal theories: The Waiver Doctrine applies when the IRS investigates the merits of a technically defective refund claim as if it were formal, thereby waiving procedural compliance (Angelus Milling Co. v. Commissioner, 325 U.S. 293 (1945); Zeeman v. United States, 395 F.2d 861 (2d Cir. 1968)). For waiver to apply, three elements are mandatory: Judge Donnelly concluded that the Waiver Doctrine did not apply. The IRS’s internal transaction codes (971 and 977) and its September 19, 2022 response letter failed to demonstrate unmistakable processing of a refund request. The IRS letter conflated the $10,700 audit issue with the $28,069.74 refund request and misapprehended her request as a demand to reduce unpaid tax liability rather than refund taxes already paid. Thus, the court held that the IRS did not unmistakably waive formal filing defects. Under the landmark precedent United States v. Kales, 314 U.S. 186 (1941), a written notice that fairly advises the IRS of the nature of a taxpayer’s claim within the statutory period—though formally defective—will be treated as a valid claim if formal defects are subsequently cured by an amendment filed after the limitation period expires. As synthesized in AmBase Corp. and United States v. Forma, 42 F.3d 759 (2d Cir. 1994), a valid informal claim requires three elements: Applying these elements, Judge Donnelly held that Ms. Singh’s July 25, 2019 letter constituted a valid, timely informal claim: Written Component: Met via the physical letter sent to the Kansas City Service Center. Notice of Refund: Although the letter used the term “waive” rather than “refund,” the court observed: “A refund is the only way the IRS can ‘waive’ a penalty that a taxpayer has already paid.” Citing McMillan v. IRS, 2010 WL 3804895 (E.D.N.Y. 2010), the court emphasized that the only reasonable construction of her request to waive taxes and penalties paid on June 14, 2018, was a claim for refund. Factual and Legal Grounds: The government contended that Ms. Singh failed to state a valid ground because she requested relief for “hardship” rather than explicitly citing a “theft loss deduction” under IRC § 165. Rejecting this rigid standard, the court held that tax law does not require magic words: “The plaintiff did not use the magic words ‘theft loss deduction,’ but it is clear that she was requesting one. Her letter said that she ‘was a victim of an online dating scam and was scammed [her] entire savings and [her] IRA account’ and that she ‘reached out to the NYC police to recover [her] losses and was unsuccessful.’” To perfect an informal claim, the taxpayer must submit a formal claim (Form 1040-X) while the informal claim remains pending (Computervision Corp. v. United States, 445 F.3d 1355 (Fed. Cir. 2006)). The formal amendment must relate to the same operative facts (St. Joseph Lead Co. v. United States, 299 F.2d 348 (2d Cir. 1962)). The court held that Ms. Singh’s October 19, 2022 Form 1040-X and accompanying cover letters successfully perfected the July 25, 2019 informal claim. Under 303 W. 42nd St. Enterprises, Inc. v. IRS, 181 F.3d 272 (2d Cir. 1999), a formal claim need only set forth facts sufficient to allow an intelligent review. Quoting Scovill Mfg. Co. v. Fitzpatrick, 215 F.2d 567 (2d Cir. 1954), Judge Donnelly noted that Ms. Singh “showed the actual happenings with reasonable precision, and the government taxing authorities could not have been misled by the trivial mislabeling.” Furthermore, the court firmly rejected the government’s argument that attached cover letters could not be considered because they were not under penalty of perjury. Judge Donnelly highlighted that the signature block on Form 1040-X explicitly incorporates all “accompanying schedules and statements” under penalties of perjury, and affirmed that under AmBase Corp., refund claims must be evaluated by examining surrounding communications as a whole. As an independent, alternative ground for jurisdiction, the court addressed whether the October 19, 2022 Form 1040-X was timely on its face under IRC § 7508A(d) (2019 version), which governs mandatory disaster extensions. Under the 2019 version of IRC § 7508A(d)(1), in the case of a qualified taxpayer in a federally declared disaster area, the period beginning on the earliest incident date and ending 60 days after the latest incident date specified in the declaration “shall be disregarded in the same manner as a period specified under subsection (a).” On March 20, 2020, President Trump declared a major disaster in New York starting January 20, 2020, “and continuing.” On February 10, 2023, FEMA published a notice closing the incident period for COVID-19 major disaster declarations effective May 11, 2023 (88 Fed. Reg. 8884). Sixty days following May 11, 2023, was July 10, 2023. The government raised five distinct arguments attempting to restrict the extension, all of which Judge Donnelly systematically rejected: Finally, the government asserted that even if the Form 1040-X was timely, IRC § 6511(b)(2)(A) restricted the refundable amount to taxes paid within three years prior to filing (June 14, 2018 to October 19, 2022 being greater than 3 years). Judge Donnelly rejected this defense, holding that under IRC § 7508A(a) and (d), the statutory disaster period must be disregarded in calculating the lookback window. Excluding the COVID-19 disaster period, Ms. Singh’s payment on June 14, 2018 fell comfortably within the statutory lookback period. The District Court concluded that subject matter jurisdiction existed under 28 U.S.C. § 1346(a)(1) and IRC § 7422(a) under two independent grounds: Accordingly, the court DENIED the government’s Rule 12(b)(1) motion to dismiss. title: This Lowered Chevy Silverado 1500 Is a 675-HP V-8 Street Truck That’ll Please El Camino Fans - Car and Driver
content: More lateral grip, better off-the-line traction, and an available supercharged punch with a factory-backed warranty. Established nearly 50 years ago, Fox Factory has established itself as a billion-dollar company with expertise in everything from mountain bikes to trophy trucks. For the most part, Fox builds parts to help its customers land safely after taking flight over a suitably tempting hill of dirt or sand dune. However, as observed by rapper Flo Rida, sometimes a Fox likes to get low. Such is the case with the new Lowered Chevrolet Silverado Black Widow SR, which is exactly what it says it is. Similar to Fox Factory's Ram 1500 Lowered, a street-style truck launched last year, the Silverado Lowered brings a three-inch suspension drop, available supercharged V-8 power, and massive lateral grip from 305-series rubber mounted on 22-inch wheels. A Camaro with a pickup bed? Well, it’s not like GM’s making the El Camino anymore. Plus, while there are plenty of lifted Silverados on the road these days, most of them see a lot more tarmac than gravel. Fox Factory's take on a Silverado street truck maintains its 1980-pound payload and 13,300-pound max towing capacity, so you can still haul your vintage Nova dragster to the track. The truck’s body comes with flares to fit those wide tires, a custom grille and other trimmings, and a rowdy cat-back exhaust. The standard truck features a 355-hp 5.3-liter V-8. But for those who want a lot more oomph, there’s an optional supercharged 6.2-liter V-8 that brings the muscle up to 675 horsepower and 655 pound-feet of torque. Fox has also reinforced the suspension to reduce wheel hop on hard launches. The interior has also been suitably upgraded, with available quilted diamond leather and black widow spider embossed seats. While the Black Widow starts at $84,685, the supercharged version clears $101K, and that can climb even higher if you spring for the $4895 Brembo brake upgrade, the $2895 retractable tonneau cover, or one of the myriad $9000-plus paint options. Basically, there seems to be no upper limit to what people are willing to spend on a luxury-class pickup, and this factory-supported effort looks to take advantage of that niche. Cadillac might want to consider taking another crack at the EXT. In the meantime, this Fox Factory truck can be serviced at any Chevrolet dealership, and it comes with a three-year, 36,000-mile warranty. As an alternative to building your own street-style Chevy pickup with aftermarket parts, it’s a well-thought-out package with solid factory support. Set your expectations low, and hit the road. Archives Carolyn V. Craine passed away peacefully at home in Ormond Beach, Florida, with family present at the age of 95. She was the oldest of seven siblings. She helped raise them as her parents farmed in northwest Ohio. She was a high school band majorette and promoted twirling with her two girls. She met her husband, John, while roller skating. She became a stay-at-home mom until she went to beauty school and opened a salon in her home. She was a techie at heart buying a microwave, laptop , cell and caption call phone. She loved vacations in Ormond Beach, Florida and eventually purchased an oceanfront condo which was shared with family for short vacations. She became a snowbird traveling back and forth from Ohio. She was known for her friendliness and elegance. She promoted patriotism, veterans and love of country frequently wearing red, white and blue and flying the American flag. She is survived by her two children, Connie Sue (John) Karby and Vickie Lee Craine; two step-grandchildren; three step great-grandchildren; one brother, Clayton L. You will be a lot of things, but one thing you will not be is bored. Emillia Hawkins has all the breaking news and more. As the campaign rushes to its conclusion, Tanya Aldred keeps those on tenterhooks updated with all the highs and lows, wickets and runs. Champagne corks are planned to pop at Warwickshire who are striding toward clinching the County Championship title against relegation-threatened Leicestershire at Edgbaston. A win would guarantee a first pennant since the Covid-shortened 2021 campaign, with second-placed Somerset faltering against Surrey. In Division Two promotion hopefuls Kent are battling rock-bottom Gloucestershire at Canterbury. Northamptonshire, just four points behind second-placed Kent, need to step up against Middlesex. Why not join the conversation? Azerbaijan is marking 10 years since its first F1 race but this year’s event is a little different. The grand prix is taking place on a Saturday because Sunday is a national holiday, Remembrance Day. The Baku City Circuit hosting Saturday’s race is about 105 miles from the nearest point on Azerbaijan’s southern border with Iran, yet the turmoil of the regional conflict that has accounted for other motor sport events has not shunted this fixture off the F1 calendar. Two other world championships governed by the FIA have abandoned plans to race in the Middle East this year. The World Rally Championship last week scrapped its season-ending event in Saudi Arabia after travel concerns from teams. The World Endurance Championship cancelled races in Bahrain and Qatar in July and replaced them with European venues. Azerbaijan has been less directly affected by the Iran war than the Gulf nations, many of which host major US military bases and were targeted by Iranian strikes. So, F1 racing will go on, as Kimi Antonelli commands a vast 81-point lead over his Mercedes teammate George Russell. Baku is where Oscar Piastri’s title challenge started to crumble a year ago but Antonelli’s lead is more than double the biggest advantage the McLaren driver had last year and he is coming off back-to-back wins. Dominic Booth covers the race lap-by-lap. Giles Richards reports. So to the first of Saturday’s two big games. In an extended international break, the Scots face the Slovenians twice, Switzerland and North Macedonia as they strive to get out of League B. Enter Sébastien Pocognoli, tasked with building on the groundwork laid by Steve Clarke, under whom Scotland qualified for three major tournaments, including this summer’s World Cup in North America. “We arrive in the timeline of the Scotland national team [where], in the natural way, you will have some changes. But I don’t see this as a bad challenge, I think it’s a needed challenge,” the former Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco manager said in the buildup. Those Scotland followers of a jaded nature might say t’was ever thus: a challenge. Maybe it will take a Belgian to take this generation of players to a higher level and provide some cheer for the longsuffering Tartan Army. Barry Glendenning live blogs the match, with Ewan Murray reporting from Ljubljana’s Stadion Stozice. Spain’s visit to Wembley is a painful reminder to England of what might have been, and Thomas Tuchel needs a positive response to silence criticism of how the Three Lions’ World Cup fizzled out against a snarling, brutal Argentina. Had England held out for the final five minutes plus stoppage time in their semi-final two months ago, they would have met Spain in the final. Instead Tuchel’s players wilted, conceding twice after he had attempted to batten down the hatches with a series of defensive substitutions. The German coach admitted to being left “unfulfilled” by failing to achieve his target of a second star on the England jersey. Bukayo Saka went even further in midweek by revealing “there’s still a scar in us” over what happened in Atlanta. Time to start healing those wounds against the best international team on the planet. It is a tall order, particularly with a string of high-profile withdrawals. Rob Smyth will keep the blog updates flowing while our top team of David Hytner, Barney Ronay and Jacob Steinberg provide reports and analysis from the national stadium. Matchday live returns with more buildup, breaking news, good vibes and reader comments, with Billy Munday, Will Unwin and Yara El-Shaboury keeping it all flowing. There will be the latest updates on Manchester City v the Premier League and wash-up from England and Scotland’s Nations League clashes, as well as looking forward to Sunday’s key clashes: Israel v Ireland, Denmark v Wales, Serbia v Netherlands, Germany v Greece and Norway v Portugal. There is no better place to start your footballing day. Join the conversation by emailing your thoughts and queries to matchday.live@theguardian.com Rob Smyth and Tim de Lisle have over-by-over coverage of the third ODI after Sri Lanka levelled the series in thrilling last-over fashion at Headingley on Thursday. England were cruising to a target of 322 while Tom Banton (73) and Ben Duckett (67) shared a first-wicket stand of 143. Sri Lanka had been hammered 3-0 in a preceding T20 campaign but Dunith Wellalage dragged them back by removing both openers and captain Harry Brook to reduce England to 157 for three. The left-arm spinner finished with figures of three for 49 after captain Kusal Mendis hit a fine century. The teams now head to London for a series-decider at the Oval. In the aftermath Brook insisted this was just what England needed before next year’s 50-over World Cup in southern Africa. “We’ve got a great opportunity now to try to win this series, and a great opportunity for 12 months’ time,” he said. “In pressure situations, like the one that awaits us at the Oval, it will be great to see where we are as a team.” Our cricket correspondent Ali Martin reports. The season’s final day – will it be Warks? Or will Somerset gatecrash the pennant party? Tanya Aldred is back to steer the live blog as the domestic campaign hurtles to the grandest of grandstand finishes. Join her for all the latest developments. Renée Slegers’ unbeaten Arsenal face their derby rivals at Stamford Bridge after draws against Crystal Palace and Manchester United. However, only two goals and five points from three WSL matches is a telling indication of their season so far. Yet Tuesday’s 1-0 Champions League victory over HB Køge was achieved while several first-choice players were rested. They should be back in red and white for one of the campaign’s blockbusters as the two most successful clubs in the WSL era collide. Chelsea recorded their own Champions League success in midweek, with Wieke Kapteina’s strike securing 1-0 win over Austria Vienna, having struggled to impose themselves over Birmingham City last weekend. Will Unwin hosts the live blog, with Sophie Downey reporting. Buckle up, NFL fans: Graham Searles’ rolling blog is the best way to follow all the unfurling action on a Sunday evening. He’ll be focusing on two of week three’s key games: Dolphins v Chiefs and Bills v Chargers. Miami lost to San Francisco 49ers last time out – unraveling in the second half of an eventual 35-13 defeat – and face another tough challenge when the three-time Super Bowl MVP Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs visit. The Chiefs are off to a 2-0 flyer, thanks largely to a balanced offence bolstered by the former Seattle running back Kenneth Walker III. The reigning Super Bowl MVP began the season with consecutive games of more than 175 scrimmage yards, creating room for Mahomes to have more success through the air. The Chiefs are averaging an NFL-best 457.5 yards through two games, which is about 137 more than their per-game average last season. Likewise, Buffalo are rolling after two straight wins, while the Los Angeles Chargers are winless as they hit the road for Sunday’s game. John Brewin has rolling coverage of Sunday evening’s big internationals, and he’ll be zeroing in on the Republic of Ireland’s troubled clash in Hungary. The Irish face Israel before a designated “home” game in Serbia on 4 October, amid protests and calls for a boycott over Israel’s war in Gaza. The country’s strong support for the Palestinian cause dictates there will be no Irish supporters in the stadium, no home match in Ireland, and no pundits or Irish commentary on television. The game is being staged in Debrecen because Israel cannot host international matches. Ireland’s manager, Heimir Hallgrimsson, raised tension levels last week by saying that many of his squad were uncomfortable about taking part, adding: “We’re not playing with genocide, we’re playing against genocide.” Those comments drew a furious response from the Israel Football Association, which accused Hallgrimsson of “hypocrisy and stupidity”.

content: IRVING, Texas - San José State linebacker and special-teams standout John Norwood has been named a semifinalist for the prestigious 2026 William V. The Campbell Trophy® recognizes an individual as the nation's premier football scholar-athlete for combined academic success, football performance, and exemplary leadership. Norwood, an Aviation major, former walk-on, and a Milpitas, Calif., native, is one of the Mountain West Conference's most decorated scholar-athletes, with a cumulative GPA just under 4.0. title: Manchester City v Premier League: how the legal teams lined up - The Guardian
content: David Pannick may not earn as much as Erling Haaland but the club spared no expense to defend themselves against more than 100 charges The result is finally in from a highly anticipated Premier League match-up: the legal battle which pitted the league against Manchester City, the team that have dominated the competition in recent years. As befitting such a heavyweight clash, both sides fielded an impressive team of lawyers, which lined up as follows: Leading the City team was David Pannick KC, one of the foremost barristers of his generation, renown for representing the rich and powerful. Previous clients include Queen Elizabeth II, Boris Johnson, the kingdom of Saudi Arabia and more than one billionaire sheikh. Lawyers may not earn as much as the Erling Haaland’s £500,000 a week but Pannick charges a none too shoddy £5,000 an hour. In 2019, Pannick charged £407,250 for defending Sheikh Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber al-Thani, a former Qatari prime minister, involving a two-day trial, which the crossbench peer did not attend. Paul Harris KC, a leading sport and commercial silk, also led City’s successful appeal before the court of arbitration for sport (Cas) against Uefa’s Champions League ban on the club for alleged breaches of financial fair play rules. He is said to have been a trusted adviser to the club for more than 20 years. Another silk on the team was Philip Marshall KC, who specialises in complex commercial disputes and commercial fraud, and the magic circle law firm Clifford Chance is also involved. Adam Lewis KC is widely regarded as the country’s preeminent sports barrister and co-authored the leading textbook in the field. His significant cases include acting for Chelsea at Cas when they successfully halved a two-transfer-window ban imposed by Fifa. He also represented Premiership Rugby at an independent tribunal where the champions Saracens were found to have breached salary cap regulations. Andrew Hunter KC’s prominent sports cases include rugby’s “bloodgate” scandal and Formula One’s spygate scandal when McLaren were fined $100m (then £50m) and docked all their points in the constructors’ championship when found in possession of documents belonging to Ferrari. Jason Pobjoy KC represented the Premier League alongside Lewis as he did when Everton were docked points for breaching financial rules. Pobjoy argued that Everton’s “unreasonable conduct in the proceedings unnecessarily and significantly increased” costs for the league, which sought to recover £4.9m in lawyers’ fees. However, Everton argued the costs were “eye-watering” and were ordered to pay only £1.7m. Pobjoy has also represented the Football Association but is best known for his civil liberties, public and human rights law cases, including substantial pro bono work.

V (NASDAQ: IPEX) ("Inflection Point"), a special purpose acquisition company (the "Business Combination"). The Business Combination was approved by Inflection Point shareholders in a special meeting held on September 3, 2026 and formally closed on September 25, 2026. The new combined company will operate as "GOWell Energy Technology" ("GOWell Energy"). On September 28, 2026, GOWell Energy's ordinary shares will begin trading on the NASDAQ under the ticker symbol "GOW". Concurrently with the closing of the Business Combination, GOWell completed the previously announced Closing PIPE investment, pursuant to which the investor purchased approximately $50 million of preferred shares and warrants of GOWell Energy. Together with the approximately $20 million private placement funded at the signing of the Business Combination Agreement in October 2025, the PIPE investments provided GOWell Energy with $70 million of gross proceeds, before deducting transaction fees and expenses, to support GOWell Energy's growth initiatives and working capital. Guillaume Borrel, GOWell's CEO, commented: "The completion of our business combination caps 19 years of building GOWell into a wireline solutions developer and provider that service companies and operators can depend on downhole. Going public on NASDAQ gives us access to capital and the visibility to scale our sensing platform. GOWell's technologies are mission critical to safely and efficiently securing energy sources, enabling us to deliver solutions faster to both traditional and energy transition markets in this time of increased energy volatility." Michael Blitzer, Chairman and CEO of Inflection Point, added: "For nearly two decades, GOWell has developed technologically advanced equipment, software and data analytics that have helped the world's leading oilfield services companies address increasingly complex challenges. This has led to a resilient, cash-generative business with a track record of growth and margin expansion through industry cycles. As a public company, GOWell's experienced executive team is poised to accelerate growth and consolidate its leading position in a fragmented industry." Cantor Fitzgerald & Co. and Cohen & Company Capital Markets, a division of Cohen & Company Securities, LLC, served as lead financial and capital markets advisors to Inflection Point. White & Case LLP served as legal counsel to Inflection Point, and Hunter Taubman Fischer & Li LLC served as legal counsel to GOWell. Conyers Dill & Pearman served as Cayman Islands counsel to Inflection Point and Ogier (Cayman) LLP served as Cayman Islands counsel to GOWell. Gateway Group served as investor relations and public relations advisor for the transaction. The Company has a global, diverse customer base with long-term relationships with the key major oil service companies and operators in the energy sector. title: Brown Named Semifinalist for William V. Campbell Trophy - georgiastatesports.com
content: ATLANTA — Georgia State senior quarterback Cameran Brown has been named one of 206 semifinalists for the 2026 William V. Campbell Trophy®, the National Football Foundation (NFF) & College Hall of Fame announced Wednesday. Celebrating its 37th year, the Campbell Trophy recognizes the nation's premier football scholar-athlete for combined academic success, football performance and exemplary leadership. Brown was selected as Georgia State's sole nominee for the award and joins a record-setting group of 206 semifinalists from across all NCAA divisions and the NAIA. The group includes 95 student-athletes from the Football Bowl Subdivision. The senior quarterback has continued to lead the Panthers both on and off the field in 2026. Through three games, Brown has completed 61-of-90 passes for 725 yards and four touchdowns while completing 67.8 percent of his attempts and posting a 143.4 efficiency rating. Brown has accounted for 819 yards of total offense through the first three games of the season, representing 53.5 percent of Georgia State's 1,531 total yards. Most recently, Brown turned in his best passing performance of the season at UCF, setting season highs with 30 completions, 47 attempts, 282 passing yards and two touchdown passes. Brown opened the season by completing 15-of-20 passes for 190 yards and two touchdowns in Georgia State's win over North Carolina A&T on Sept. 4. He connected with DJ Murray for a 30-yard touchdown for the Panthers' first score of the season. The William V. Campbell Trophy semifinalists are nominated by their respective institutions, with each school limited to one nominee. Candidates must be a senior in their final year of eligibility or a graduate student or graduate transfer who has already earned a degree, maintain a cumulative undergraduate GPA of at least 3.2, be a significant contributor on the football field and demonstrate strong leadership and citizenship. This year's 206 semifinalists boast an average GPA of 3.64, with 98 having already earned their bachelor's degrees. The group also features 130 team captains, 24 All-Americans and 114 all-conference selections. The Campbell Trophy is part of the NFF National Scholar-Athlete Awards Presented by Fidelity Investments, now in its 68th year. The program has recognized 954 individuals and will surpass $13.5 million in postgraduate scholarships with this year's awards. The NFF will announce 12 to 16 finalists on Oct. 21. Each finalist will receive an $18,000 postgraduate scholarship and become a member of the 2026 NFF National Scholar-Athlete Class Presented by Fidelity Investments. The finalists will be honored at the 68th NFF Annual Awards Dinner on Dec. 8 at the Bellagio Resort & Casino in Las Vegas. One finalist will be selected as the recipient of the 37th William V. Campbell Trophy and will have his postgraduate scholarship increased to $25,000. The Campbell Trophy was first awarded in 1990 and has become one of college football's most prestigious honors for achievement on the field, in the classroom and in the community. title: Czechia v Spain: How the tie was won - Billie Jean King Cup
content: Are the good times about to roll again? Czechia have surged into their first Billie Jean King Cup by Gainbridge final since 2018 – the last time they were crowned champions in the women’s World Cup of Tennis. Their last title bookended a period of domination in this competition when Czechia, under the captaincy of Petr Pala, built something of a Billie Jean King Cup dynasty. One of Pala’s chief lieutenants, Barbora Strycova, is now sitting on the Czechia bench after taking over as captain ahead of April’s Qualifiers and she could be about to end her nation’s wait for silverware. In terms of Strycova’s CV, the 40-year-old represented Czechia in Billie Jean King Cup between 2002 and 2018 and is one of five players in the competition’s history to win it six or more times, doing so in 2011-12, 2014-16 and 2018. What a record and Czechia have taken a big step towards the promised land once again, with Billie Jean King Cup silverware now tantalisingly within reach following victory over Spain in what was their first semi-final since 2023. Defeat will be disappointing for Spain but, under the stewardship of captain Carla Suarez Navarro, they have made significant progress this season, with this their first semi-final in nearly two decades. This Czechia team has real strength and great options, and despite a commanding quarter-final victory over Great Britain, Strycova opted to shuffle her pack with Karolina Muchova chosen to contest the opening singles match. It is always pleasing for a captain to be able to replace quality with quality, and drafting in Muchova – currently ranked No. 8 in the WTA Rankings – is a reflection of Strycova’s position of power. This was two-time Grand Slam finalist Muchova’s first taste of Billie Jean King Cup action since the 2022 Finals and she rose to the occasion, dispatching Jessica Bouzas Maneiro, 7-5 6-4. Bouzas Maneiro has not won back-to-back matches since reaching the third round at Wimbledon, and she was unable to buck that trend here and replicate Wednesday's victory over Kazakhstan's Sonja Zhiyenbayeva. The 24-year-old did have her moments and led in the first set, only for Muchova to find her feet, and once a player of such quality has a grasp on proceedings it is difficult to loosen that grip. Muchova’s success put Czechia 1-0 up in the tie ahead of the second singles match, and Spanish morale will not have been boosted by the sight of Linda Noskova, who boasts a six-match winning streak in the competition, striding to the court. Czechia were now just one win from sealing their place in the final and Noskova is a tough nut to crack. Spain were very much up against it. However, as in the first singles match, Cristina Bucsa did not stand on ceremony. World No. 35 Bucsa took the fight to Noskova and recovered to force a first-set tie-break, only for Noskova to find the necessary inspiration to repel the Spanish threat once backed into a corner. The second set was more of a formality as Noskova triumphed 7-6(5) 6-2 to ensure that Czechia will once again battle for honours in Billie Jean King Cup – the largest annual women’s international team competition in sport. In the first set of the opening singles match, Bouzas Maneiro was playing well and making her presence felt against a player ranked 85 places above her in the WTA Rankings. Bouzas Maneiro had two break points for a 5-3 lead only for Muchova to recover and hold serve. The Czech then won three of the next four games to claim the opening set. Entering this clash, Bouzas Maneiro had lost her last 10 matches when dropping the opening set – and there was no way back in this one despite her early momentum. Muchova never gave a backward glance and powered to victory. Nobody can see into the future, but Czechia would have every confidence in Wimbledon champion and world No. 6 Noskova doing the business in the second singles match. If Spain were going to strike, they perhaps needed something from the opening singles. Bucsa’s tail was up after forcing a first-set tie-break in the second singles and led 4-2 as five-time champions Spain desperately tried to claw their way back into proceedings. However, the outcome of games, sets and matches can turn on one shot and a ferocious cross-court forehand stoked the flames of a Noskova revival as she fired back to take the set. When opportunities present themselves, particularly against quality operators such as Noskova, they need to be taken. Easier said than done, but this was a key play, and one which could have turned the tide in Spain’s favour had it gone their way. Less of a statistic, more of a factoid. Noskova grew up idolising former world No. 2 and two-time Grand Slam champion Petra Kvitova – and who can blame her? Kvitova won six Billie Jean King Cup titles as a player with Czechia, and this is relevant because Noskova may be about to follow in the footsteps of her heroine and the person she looked up to as a child. Dynasty is the word – it has been used in this piece, in fact – when considering those glory-filled years Czechia had in this competition. Of course, they have to get over the line in Sunday’s final first, but Czechia could well be embarking on a new era of success. Strycova (Czechia captain): “To be in the final as a captain after being in this position for one year, if someone would have told me this, I would not have believed. But, with this team that I have, it is possible. “The last step we have is on Sunday. I feel like everybody wants it so much. We have the chance to lift the trophy. The last time we were in the final was 2018, which was my last year in Billie Jean King Cup as a player. It is surreal but, at the same time, very real.” Noskova: “We definitely want to make our captain proud. As she said, the last time we won it, she was on the team. It would be quite beautiful to have her part of the team and win it once again, just from a different position. “But I always love to play for the team no matter what. No matter the circumstances or whether we’re playing at the Finals or in the Qualifiers, nothing changes for me.” Muchova: “It was very special for me to win the opening singles match. It has been a while since I played Billie Jean King Cup, so to bring the first point to our locker was important. It gave Linda some air, so she didn't feel so much pressure." “It is very special for us to play the final and going one step further would be even more special, especially with Czechia having such a big history and the girls from the other generation winning it so many times. It would definitely be special for us to win it.” Suarez Navarro (Spain captain): “I am really proud of my players for the way they fought and for the way they competed. They are also all together and have the same goal – the same dream. “We lost today, but I am proud of them. This year we have taken a step forward, but we have to work and we have to improve. I know how difficult this competition is.” Bouzas Maneiro: “I knew that I was playing against Karolina Muchova – she is honestly one of my favourite players on Tour. She's so talented and I really like to watch her play. “Me and my coach, we always talk about how talented she is and how she plays. It is beautiful to watch her playing tennis. When I knew that I was playing against her, I was happy for that because I wanted to play against the player that she is.” Czechia will contest Sunday’s final, so for the time being they can sit back and relax having done all they can. The second semi-final between defending champions Italy, who are looking to win their third successive Billie Jean King Cup title, and Ukraine will take place on Saturday. Maybe Czechia will be interested observers or perhaps they will choose to stay away and focus on their own preparations and gameplan. Either way, a fascinating few days are about to unfold. For Czechia, opportunity knocks on Sunday.

title: Cadillac, Ford, and Their F1 Rivals Are Still Waiting on Talks About Switching to V-8s - Road & Track
content: Manufacturers still have “no clarity” ahead of the much-anticipated return to substantial internal combustion power from eight-cylinder engines. The debate over the next generation of Formula 1 engines continues to tick away in the background of the current season—and in the words of Audi boss Mattia Binotto, there is still “no clarity” on where things are going. One thing is clear, and that is that F1 will return to a V-8. That means getting away from the controversial and unpopular battery-dominated technology that the sport currently finds itself stuck with. Both the FIA and F1 have made it clear that V-8s are the way forward, and the teams and manufacturers have agreed in principle. The question marks are over the details of the new regulations, and specifically, the timing. In theory, the current format runs until 2030; after that, the FIA can pretty much write the rules it wants for 2031. However, there is a lot of momentum behind fast-tracking the change to 2030, dumping the current formula a year early. The difficulty with that is two-fold. First, an early change needs support from all stakeholders. Secondly, while 2030 seems like it’s far away, it’s anything but when it comes to power unit design. We are fast approaching a point where the manufacturers simply would not be able to be ready for 2030. It’s a particularly big call for Cadillac; the teams intends to switch from a Ferrari supply to its own GM power unit—but does it do so under the current rules, or hold out for the V-8 era and a clean-sheet start for everyone? “There is no clarity yet,” Binotto said in Baku on Thursday. “So, we know that FIA is still elaborating what may be the concepts they would like to propose. We know it’s a V-8 for certain, 2030 the earliest introduction. On the timing, if it would be 2030, what does it mean in terms of starting the development? It has to be very soon. It has to be before the end of the year. I think the regulation needs to be agreed and voted before the end of the year to have certain clarities, by 2027, to start really the design and concept phase.” The obvious aim of the change is to improve the racing, while also keeping a lid on spending—something that all the manufacturers are keen to see. “What’s the main objective we are looking at?,” Binotto noted. “I think we all agree, first will be a significant cost saving required. The current power unit is still very expensive, and we believe that having a clear target on cost would be important. When considering the format of the V-8 itself, we believe that we still need to retain some advanced technologies.” And that is a big part of the debate—how much tech will be part of the package, with some manufacturers wanting more than others. “I think that F1 has always been the edge of the platform for innovation, and we believe whatever will be the overall format, it has to remain a platform for innovation for all the manufacturers,” said Binotto. “So yes, welcome the V-8, welcome a better sound, welcome a cost saving. And when it comes into the details of hybrid, I would say yes, turbo, possibly yes. But all the details, I think, need to be discussed with the FIA. That’s why I think that discussion will start very soon.” Red Bull boss Laurent Mekies, who is fighting Ford’s corner with the in-house PU project, is confident that agreement will be reached. “I think we are at the point where all the manufacturers ... I don’t think we have very different ideas or very opposite ideas about what we all want from it,” said the Frenchman. “I think we want flat-out racing, flat-out qualifying. That will probably dictate the next architecture. And as Mattia said, you want flat-out racing, flat-out qualifying and retaining the technological challenge and the technological laboratories. And of course, we would like to do that also by ticking a few of the boxes.” Mekies is confident that a consensus will be found. “I think in terms of these high level objectives, with the FIA, with F1, with the teams, I think we are all pretty aligned,” he said. “And how do you do it in the details, with the various options we have, it will be the discussion over the next few months. But in terms of what we want to achieve as stakeholders of the sport, I think we are all quite aligned.” In the meantime, the sport has to make the best of the current regulations, which have at least three further years to run. There are already changes coming, with a greater internal combustion focus relative to the battery from 2027 courtesy of higher fuel flow. This week, it was formally agreed that races will be two or three laps shorter to create the scope to use that fuel without creating having to create bigger tank capacity, thus allowing teams to carry over their 2026 chassis designs. In the meantime, fierce critics of the current rules want to see even more change. Champions Max Verstappen and Fernando Alonso are among the most vocal in that group. “Next year there is a change already with the 60-40 ratio, and that I think will improve things,” Alonso said in Baku. “But maybe there are more things that we need to think about, to keep improving things. That's the way I see it, and that's part of my responsibility as well. I drove long enough here, and I think we all come from junior formulas, from karting, F3, F2, that we drive within this driver instinct to go fast, attacking the corners and taking some risk. And then you get to F1 and you need to rewind a little bit what you learn in the last 20 years of your career, and then you need to drive a different method. That is only happening in F1. There is no other series in motorsport that you need to drive slow to go fast…” “The road map is a clear step forward compared to where we are here, with a rather small step next year and a significant step for 2028,” said Mekies. “As Oracle Red Bull Racing, we will support further tweaks if there is an agreement to further tweaks in the directions of flat-out qualifying, flat-out racing, which I think is what Fernando and Max were probably mentioning. Yes, we will support.” “Obviously, what Fernando or Max said, I don’t know, needs to be evaluated,” said Binotto. “I think the concept certainly is to try always to improve the regulation. For ’27, already a significant change will happen, and I think first we need to go through that change, and see what will be the result of the changes we’ve made in terms of flat out racing, et cetera. So, I would be patient. I would wait to see first how much the changes we have, which are somehow significant, how much those changes will improve the situation, to furthermore, let me say, modify. And again, as Laurent said, we are always open for constructive discussions if further tuning would be required.” We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we back.

title: GM Unveils New 555-HP Duramax 8.3-liter Turbo-Diesel V-8 - The ClassicCars.com Journal
content: The 555-horsepower Duramax 8.3-liter Turbo-Diesel V-8 and updates to the capable 6.6-liter V-8 gas engine have arrived. The new horsepower, torque, and features might have prospective GM customers wondering, “If back in the day we could deliver pizzas in 30 minutes or less, maybe with 555 horsepower and 1,230 lb-ft of torque, we can do the same with freight!” Of course, those pesky things called laws and regulations might get in the way of optimism for many operators. “For 2027, we took GM’s proven HD validation playbook and turned up the capability — integrating new powertrain, braking, steering and chassis technologies for serious customers who push their trucks hard every day,” said Mark Dickens, Executive Chief Engineer for GM Full Size Trucks and SUVs. “HD customers don’t hold back — and neither did we.” The new Duramax 8.3-liter Turbo-Diesel V-8 offers 555 horsepower and 1,230 lb-ft of torque. In case you’re curious like I was, Ford’s 2027 High-Output 6.7-liter Power Stroke V-8 is currently rated at 500 horsepower and 1,200 lb-ft of torque. GM’s enhanced 6.6-liter V-8 gas engine is rated at 412 horsepower and 472 lb-ft of torque when installed in heavy-duty pickups. Earlier this week, General Motors put out a teaser video that took a direct shot at Ford. Mentioning, “a certain crosstown rival’s HD V-8 diesel engine may be referred to as the ‘Scorpion.’ But nature — or GM, in this case — always engineers a better predator: the Mongoose. Built to dominate, this diesel engine packs power, capability, and confidence.” For those unaware, Scorpion is Ford’s nickname for its 6.7-liter Power Stroke V-8. “This new diesel engine is the culmination of decades of GM diesel development and integration,” said Norman Peralta, Executive Chief Engineer, Global Engine and Battery Systems. “From the clean-sheet architecture and combustion system to the cooling, aftertreatment and transmission calibration, this is a powertrain built with heavy-duty purpose and pride.” In addition to the impressive performance specifications, the new Duramax is “engineered as a holistically integrated system to deliver more power, control and confidence for customers who demand maximum capability from their trucks every day.” The engine will be paired with the Allison 10-speed 10L1000 transmission equipped with “advanced shift logic.” GM’s latest diesel engine includes the following benefits: The Duramax will be built at GM’s DMAX facility in Brookville, Ohio, which recently received a $920 million investment from General Motors to support high-volume production of diesel engines. The 6.6-liter V-8 gas engine will be built at GM’s Tonawanda Engine Plant in New York. The new drivetrain is capable of towing up to 38,000 pounds and has a gross combined weight rating of up to 46,500 pounds. All that capacity is well handled thanks to updated trailering technology and upgraded undercarriage components which include a new state-of-the-art heavy-duty braking system and proprietary rack-and-pinion electric power steering system. The “segment-first” electronic brake-boost system includes 14.6-inch front rotors, four-piston fixed front calipers, and upgraded rear hardware for improved thermal capacity. GM also designed the system to have a new pedal position that promotes less pedal travel for a more predictable feel. In previous models, the braking and power steering systems would share one hydraulic source; for the 2027s, this was eliminated to reduce complexity, remove weight, and improve on- and off-road steering at lower speeds. So if the power steering isn’t run off hydraulics, how does it work? I’m glad you asked, Mr. or Mrs. Ghost. The previous hydraulically assisted steering system has been replaced with a rack-and-pinion electric power steering system “designed specifically for heavy-duty truck demands.” GM went in and eliminated hydraulic pumps, hoses, fluid, and related hardware to reduce traditional steering noise, lower complexity, and, of course, “improve the ownership experience.” The hardware is corrosion- and impact-resistant for job sites that may include rough terrain, road debris, and “severe-duty use.” These new engines will be available in 2027 Chevrolet Silverado HD and GMC Sierra HD pickups, which are expected to arrive at U.S. dealerships in late 2026. Pricing has not yet been announced. Growing up, Corey Decker spent time with his dad in the garage building muscle cars as a hobby. He also acquired intimate familiarity with classics new and old as the lead Car Description Editor at AutoHunter.com before segueing into The ClassicCars.com Journal. In a previous life, he worked as a sportswriter and even scored the opportunity to cover the 2016 Olympics. A sucker for diesel pickups and long Cadillacs, Corey’s dream car is a 1969 Ford Mustang Boss 429. Your email address will not be published. title: Uefa Nations League today: How to watch Turkey v France, TV channels & live stream Friday 25 September - The Guardian
content: How will Turkey and France fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options After 14 years of ‘Deschamps-ball,’ France will start a new era under Zinedine Zidane against Turkey in the Uefa Nations League with the new Les Bleus manager calling up several new faces to his squad. Kylian Mbappé has described working under Zidane as “like something from a movie” although the Real Madrid forward is an injury doubt for Friday’s game. Turkey are hoping to bounce back from a disappointing World Cup that saw Vincenzo Montella’s side crash out in the group stage. Here is your complete guide on how to watch today’s Uefa Nations League fixture, including kick-off times, broadcast networks, and online streaming options. Zidane has long been a mystery as a manager. While the former midfielder enjoyed incredible success as Real Madrid boss, winning three Champions League titles, his favoured style of play wasn’t always obvious. He has always been a vibes over tactics coach. Didier Deschamps was never renowned for his tactical acumen either and so Zidane’s appointment may not represent much of a shift for Les Bleus. Nonetheless, there is intrigue over how France’s players will respond to a new manager after such a long time playing for Deschamps. Montella kept his job as Turkey manager despite his team’s disastrous World Cup campaign, although the Italian is under pressure. Hakan Calhanoglu will be missed in central midfield, but Turkey still have a lot of talent in other areas. Player to watch: Kylian Mbappé, France - Assuming Mbappé shakes off an injury to feature, he will be France’s primary attacking threat as he has been for the last decade. The 27-year-old has scored eight goals in eight games this season and could add to that individual tally against Turkey.

title: John V. "Jack" Cannon III - Sarasota Herald-Tribune
content: John V. (“Jack”) Cannon, III died at home Sunday, September 20, 2026, after an extended illness. Jack Cannon was born in Houston, Texas on May 24th 1945, and spent most of his childhood in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. He graduated from Union College, where he was a leader both on and off the football field, and then attended the Florida State University College of Law. He moved to Sarasota to join the Williams, Parker Law Firm in 1972. It is tempting, particularly when someone has been as successful in their career as Jack was, to describe their professional accomplishments and accolades as if that success was the measure of the man. It is seldom a complete picture, but that is especially true with Jack. He was, of course, a brilliant lawyer—a zealous advocate, an insightful counselor and tactician, a tough negotiator, and a loyal and trustworthy partner. He was also an extraordinary mentor to generations of lawyers at Williams, Parker, from which he retired in 2014. While all of these things are accurate, Jack’s true singularity in the world, and where he made his most indelible mark, was in the scope and scale of his generosity, his capacity for joy, his boundless hospitality, and his love for his community, his friends, and—above all—his family. Jack’s life was defined by his generosity. He shared everything he had, wanted the very best for everyone he knew, and knew no limits on what he would do for others. Many local organizations benefited from his natural proclivity for giving, particularly the American Cancer Society, where he was a long time volunteer, donor, and many-time committee member for the long-running and popular Cattle Baron’s Ball. His joy and his laughter were infectious. Jack was an endless font of jokes (some decidedly “not suitable for work,” which were invariably presaged with what he thought was the inoculating phrase, “Brenda told me this joke”). His advice and counsel were priceless. Jack was a reliable and thoughtful teacher, mentor, father, and brother to all. His guidance translated naturally to coaching, and he was a well-respected and successful Babe Ruth baseball coach in Sarasota’s legendary program. He was a shoulder to cry on (and, notably, a person to cry with—Jack was the softie to end all softies), and an ever-available friend. He had the rarest of all abilities—genuinely putting himself in someone else’s shoes. This made his guidance the best of all things—informed by his experience but tailored to your own. Jack’s hospitality was legendary. He and Brenda defined the maxim “all are welcome” as their home was a gathering place for family, friends, colleagues, and the larger community.  Ask any Sarasota police officer or fire fighter where the best gathering spot was on the hardest “first responder” holidays and it is likely that they found their way to the Cannon’s for barbecue and a swim. Similarly, generations of Sarasota High School and community league football and baseball players knew they always had a home at the Cannon’s, for an hour, a day, a week, or a year. It is impossible to talk about Jack, and the Cannons, without resorting to hyperbole—but even hyperbole fails when trying to describe who Jack was to his family. No man has ever felt luckier than Jack as Brenda’s husband. He lived in awe of the fact that she had agreed to marry him. How much he loved, respected, admired, and just plain had fun with Brenda defies description, but you knew it when you saw it—a true love match. Jack’s children were the center of his world. He never stopped talking about them and was the kind of father that every child dreams of and deserves: loving, reliable, strong, kind, trustworthy, protective—and completely committed to doing whatever was needed to help them reach their potential. They say that parents should not be their children’s friends, but as in so many things, Jack was the exception to the rule— the best dad and the best friend. Jack will be missed by his wife, Brenda, his son, Matt, daughter in law, Kim, grandsons Connor and Cooper, his brothers Frank and Bar, and scores of friends. Sarasota is a beautiful place, but it and the world are all the more beautiful for being where Jack Cannon lived. He leaves a lasting legacy of love, joy, and generosity. Jack’s family is deeply grateful for the love and support they have received from the many people whose lives he touched. In accordance with his wishes, the family will celebrate his life privately. Jack never wanted a large or formal service and honoring that request is important to those who loved him most. In lieu of flowers, the family invites those wishing to honor Jack’s memory to consider making a donation to the Sarasota High School football program at https://www.zeffy.com/en-US/donation-form/support-sarasota-football-invest-in-our-sailors Coping with grief when a traditional funeral isn't possible

title: Israel v Republic of Ireland: Jack Knight says Nations League game should not go ahead - BBC
content: Jason Knight made his Republic of Ireland debut in 2020 and has won 44 caps Jason Knight has become the first Republic of Ireland player to publicly voice his opposition to playing Israel on Sunday. The sides are due to meet in Debrecen, Hungary at 19:45 BST, with the return fixture in Backa Topola, Serbia on 4 October. Since the sides were drawn together in Group B3, there has been increasing calls in Ireland to withdraw from the games due to the ongoing war in Gaza with a 'Stop The Game' campaign gathering pace. Speaking before Thursday's 1-0 defeat by Kosovo in Pristina, Republic stand-in skipper Dara O'Shea confirmed the players would meet on Friday to discuss their approach to Sunday's 'home' game against Israel, which will have no Irish fans in attendance, before their behind-closed-doors match the following week. "Look, it's difficult, the manager, and Dara, and Nathan [Collins] spoke well about it, I don't think the game should be going ahead but it is going ahead," Knight said following the Kosovo game. "We'll have a deeper talk about it and what that means, we'll get our thoughts as a group and go from there. "I think it was a difficult one. It's obviously big talk in Ireland. I have been focusing on my football in England in the Championship. But I knew this was coming so I had a think about it." 'Don't put pressure on us' over Israel games - Ogbene Neutral venues and no 'away' fans - how Israel v Republic of Ireland became so contentious The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations (UN). "We had chats about it with the players, and more senior players on what the step will be," added Bristol City midfielder Knight. "Now we're here, we can have a really in depth talk of what that means and what the consequences are. We'll do that [on Friday] and go from there. "I am quite experienced. None of us have gone through this scenario before but I'd like to think I'm experienced, thick skin and can get through most things and that is what I will try and do. "I'll try and focus on the football as much as I can. I'll give my view and my thoughts on when I see fit, but I'll be trying to focus on the football as much as possible." title: Honda working on new hybrid for Canadian-built CR-V: report - driving.ca
content: Rumours also point to the Japanese automaker having a three-row 'Pilot XXL' crossover in the hopper You can save this article by registering for free here. Or sign-in if you have an account. The rumour mill is churning out whispers that Honda is planning out some future moves in a pair of hotly contested segments: hybrid-powered midsize crossovers; and large three-row family rigs. First up is word that the automaker is feverishly working on a revised hybrid powertrain to plug into its popular CR-V crossover. The model is presently available in such a configuration across several different trims, but talking heads are suggesting an updated variant of the electrified powertrain is on the way — and may be here very shortly. And by “here,” we mean at the Honda factory in our country. Canada is a major producer of CR-Vs, and reports suggest this new powertrain could see action on Alliston assembly lines as soon as February next year. Furthermore, the cadence of manufacturing roll-out could place Canada on the front foot of CR-V Hybrid production, with American assembly not ramping up until March. Reporters at Nikkei Asia say the new hybrid powertrain could be up to 10% more efficient whilst also cutting production costs by over a quarter. That latter point is of no small consequence, especially with North American markets in constant tariff turmoil. If the Honda group can realize 25% or more savings on the cost of a major component, that could help offset any tariff taxes — either helping its bottom line, or reasonably holding any MSRP increases. Elsewhere in the Honda lineup, rumblings have surfaced the automaker could be working on a range-topping crossover that would outstrip the Pilot in terms of overall size. This ‘Pilot XXL’ – which would almost certainly not be its production moniker – would be a good foil against machines like the Toyota Grand Highlander and Hyundai Palisade. Production isn’t expected until 2032, apparently, which is a lifetime in the car racket. Witness all the changes in Honda’s own product plans (ahem, EVs, ahem) across a much shorter span. While some might question the need for another three-row vehicle above the Pilot, there is plenty of precedent for such a model walk. Hyundai, for example, has successfully navigated selling both the Santa Fe and Palisade, both of which are boxy three-row crossovers. title: Long Road Back For Starling Thomas V Leads To Return Against 49ers - Arizona Cardinals
content:
As The Star-Spangled Banner was performed at Allegiant Stadium before the Cardinals' second preseason game, cornerback Starling Thomas V stood along the sidelines with tears streaming down his cheeks. The raw emotions flowing moments before kickoff as the game marked the final step in Thomas' recovery. That outing against the Raiders was his return game after missing the entire 2025 campaign with a torn ACL. "You imagine yourself a year ago from that time of where you were and now look at where you are," Thomas said. "It was a long road and finally being able to see the light and being able to go out there and do something you always love to do. I'm excited." The excitement reached a new level this week when he was signed to the active roster ahead of the matchup against the 49ers. Thomas, who was promoted from the practice squad after Will Johnson's injury, is expected to see action for the first time since the 2024 season finale against that same team. It brings Thomas back to his rookie season when he was inactive during the first four weeks and then strung together 12 games and seven starts in 2023. "Preparation is for the prepared and if you prepare like you're going to play every week, when that opportunity comes, you will be ready," Thomas said. "I was in the film room like I was playing in those first two weeks, and I was on the sideline coaching the guys up. It was like a second coach for them." With Johnson sidelined for the season, the dynamic of the defensive secondary will shift. The wild card in all of this is the health status of nickel corner Garrett Williams, who has practiced in a limited fashion every day since coming off the PUP list. While Williams has been out, Denzel Burke has slid into Williams' role instead of his outside corner responsibilities. "Soon, for sure," Williams said when asked about how soon he could return. "Soon. I'm looking forward to it. "It's been good to be able to get the bumps and bruises out of the way and getting used to being out on the field just playing football again," he added. If Williams can return, Burke would return to the outside, which would create the outside cornerback pairing of Burke and Max Melton. Thomas and Kei'Trel Clark will be the other options to play on the outside. Kalen King is also on the roster and is viewed as one of the better nickel options during training camp. "I felt great about our depth from the jump, and it was such a good battle in that room," defensive coordinator Nick Rallis said. "Those guys are going to step up and fill those roles." Against the 49ers, Thomas believes similar emotions will return. There was always going to be some fiery passion towards the NFC West rival after the brawl he had with former Niners wide receiver Jauan Jennings in 2024. But there will also be a moment to appreciate the journey after what he called a roller coaster of an offseason. "It has been a humbling experience and it was a time for me to evaluate myself and make sure that my process stayed the process and that I didn't change because of the circumstances and outcomes," Thomas said. "I still came to work with a smile on my face. I'm living in a prayer, so I'm excited to be back." title: ASAN Opposes Decision in Texas v. Kennedy - autisticadvocacy.org
content: The Department of Justice is a part of the government that makes sure laws are followed. We call it DOJ for short. The DOJ and a few states made another bad decision. This update talks about what they did, what just happened, and what it means for you. On August 31st, the DOJ and a few states asked a court to resolve an important lawsuit. To resolve a lawsuit means stopping the lawsuit. It also means the people suing each other agree to do things. The lawsuit the DOJ asked to resolve is called Texas v. Kennedy. Texas v. Kennedy is a lawsuit about Section 504 rules from Health and Human Services. Health and Human Services is the part of the U.S. government in charge of healthcare. We call it HHS for short. Section 504 is a part of a law from 1973. We call it 504 for short. 504 says places that get money from the government can’t discriminate against people with disabilities. Discrimination is treating people unfairly or badly because of who they are. Section 504 has rules for how the law should be followed. A rule tells the people who need to follow a law how to follow that law. Congress makes laws. That law also tells agencies to make rules for that law. Agencies are parts of the U.S. government that make rules. HHS and the DOJ are agencies. Sometimes agencies update their rules. Sometimes people call a rule a “regulation.” The DOJ decided the U.S. government should change part of the 504 rules. So HHS changed their 504 rules in 2024. This statement calls these rules the 2024 HHS 504 Rules. The 2024 HHS 504 Rules do a lot of important things. One of those things is updating the first 504 rules. Those rules are from 1978. This was the first time HHS updated the 504 rules since 1978. One of the most important things the 2024 HHS 504 Rules talked about is the integration mandate. The integration mandate is a rule that says people with disabilities have a right to live, work, and get services in the community. The integration mandate comes from 504 and the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). The ADA is like 504. It is a law that protects people with disabilities from discrimination. The 2024 HHS 504 Rules did not create the integration mandate. But the 2024 HHS 504 Rules said the integration mandate was a part of 504. Adding the integration mandate to the 504 rules makes the law stronger. The reason Section 504 got made was to stop discrimination against people with disabilities. Adding the integration mandate to the 504 rules would help stop discrimination that keeps disabled people out of the community. On September 23rd, a federal judge sided with the DOJ, HHS, and the five states in the Texas v. Kennedy lawsuit. This decision will get rid of some parts of the 2024 rules. Those parts are about the integration mandate. The decision does not get rid of all of the 2024 rules. The decision does not get rid of Section 504. It also does not get rid of the actual integration mandate. The integration mandate comes from the ADA and 504. The decision applies to all states, not just the five states that sued. This decision hurts our community. It will make it harder for people with disabilities to get the supports and services we need to live in the community. It will make it harder for people with disabilities to stay out of institutions. It will make it harder for people with disabilities to get out of institutions. But this decision does not take away the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA), Section 504, or the Olmstead decision. We still have the right to live in our communities. States are not allowed to ignore the ADA or Section 504. We deserve a government that protects our rights. We do not deserve a government that ignores our rights. ASAN demands states continue to follow the integration mandate.

title: Texas v. Kennedy Abandons Federal Commitment to Community Integration - autisticadvocacy.org
content: September 24, 2026 — Yesterday, the federal judge in the case of Texas v. Kennedy entered an order throwing out the community integration provisions of the Section 504 rule issued in 2024 by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). The order applies across the country. The Defend Community Integration Coalition (DCIC) condemns the federal government’s action resulting in this order, and urges renewed advocacy to protect our right to community integration. The agreement approved by the judge was proposed jointly by the Department of Justice (DOJ) on behalf of HHS and the states of Texas, Florida, Alaska, Louisiana, and Montana. It affects only certain parts of the 2024 rule. The case is now closed. Learn more about Texas v. Kennedy at this link. While the DOJ/HHS and states’ agreement attempts to turn back the clock, it is important to note that this agreement does not change any laws. Despite the court’s order, Section 504, the Americans with Disabilities Act, and the Supreme Court’s Olmstead decision remain in place. We continue to have the legal right to not be forced into institutions. It is very important that governors and attorneys general in every state understand that this order goes against decades of established law, and that the disability community will not go backwards. Although our legal right to live in the community remains in place, the federal government is taking away clear direction to the states that health and social services should support disabled people in community settings whenever appropriate. The removal of the community integration provisions of the HHS Section 504 rule applies to all states, not just the states that sued. Loss of this clear guidance is a serious setback for our work to ensure that people are not forced to live in institutions in order to get the services they need. Let’s be clear. Disability rights and our ability to live in our homes and our communities are in crisis. Although some states have expressed a commitment to ensuring that people with disabilities can live in the community, many states have not done so. We urge state legislatures to use this misguided and harmful ruling as a wake up call to enshrine the right of disabled people to live in their communities in state law. The rights of disabled people have been won at enormous costs by activists over the past 50 years. Disability rights are human rights. DCIC is a national coalition of organizations led by and for people with disabilities, focused on defending our right to live in the community. Stay tuned for updates from DCIC for action opportunities to defend our right to live in the community.

title: Isaiah Shirley Named Semifinalist for William V. Campbell Trophy - NC State University Athletics
content: RALEIGH, N. C. – NC State defensive lineman Isaiah Shirley is one of 206 semifinalists for the 2026 William V. Campbell Trophy ®, college football's premier scholar-athlete award. Celebrating its 37th year, the Campbell Trophy ® recognizes the nation's best football scholar-athlete for combined academic success, football performance, and exemplary leadership.Collectively, this year's 206 semifinalists include 130 team captains, 24 All-Americans, and 114 all-conference selections.Shirley is one of 14 ACC players named a semifinalist for the award. He is majoring in sport management with a minor in psychology, holds a 3.8 GPA, and plans to pursue a postgraduate degree in business finance.Last season, Shirley was named to the All-ACC Academic Football Team and has appeared on the ACC Academic Honor Roll four times. Earlier this year, Shirley was named one of four finalists for the Arthur Ashe Sports Scholars Award. Of 900+ nominees for the award, Shirley was the only football student-athlete named a finalist.Ahead of the 2026 season, his teammates voted him assistant captain. Through three games in 2026, Shirley has totaled seven tackles, including one tackle for a loss. The Wolfpack have appeared in a bowl game every season Shirley has been on the team.Shirley, an active member of the community, has spoken at numerous high schools, sharing his testimony and offering advice grounded in his beliefs. He is involved with Uplifting Athletes, an organization that uses sports to build a community that invests in the lives of people affected by rare diseases.Shirley has already appeared on the Wuerffel Trophy Watch List and the AFCA Good Works Team.The NFF will announce 12 to 16 finalists on October 21. Each finalist will receive an $18, 000 postgraduate scholarship and become a member of the 2026 NFF National Scholar- Athlete Class Presented by Fidelity Investments.The finalists will be recognized at the 68th NFF Annual Awards Dinner, presented by Las Vegas, on December 8 at the Bellagio Resort & Casino in Las Vegas. One finalist will be selected as the recipient of the 37th Campbell Trophy®, with his postgraduate scholarship increased to $25,000.The NFF National Scholar-Athlete Awards, presented by Fidelity Investments, are in their 68th year and have recognized 954 individuals. This year's scholarships will push the program's all-time distribution above $ 13 million.
